The years went by. Christmas followed close behind Christmas, leaving a festive brightness in the air long after Epiphany. Whitsun after Whitsun ran lightly across meadows dressed in flowers. Each summer holiday approached, celebrated its orgy of sunshine and fresh air, and poured fiery wine from overflowing cups. Then one day it disappeared into the setting sun. Only memory remained, sunburnt, wide-eyed, with dancing blood.

Years had gone by, and the world had ceased to be the place of wonders it once was. No thrilling imaginary horrors remained in the dark spaces behind the decaying elder-bushes, in the secretive attic rooms, or in the gloomy stone passage beneath the Klastrup road. At the lark's first trill, the hillside still flowered until purple-edged, star-like daisies and yellow buttercups hid the grass. The river still held its fantastic abundance of plants and creatures; the sand-pit still had wild cliffs, black rocks, and fragments of silvery granite. But these were merely flowers, animals, and stones. Once again the glittering fairy gold had become dead leaves.

Game after game grew stale and foolish, as dull and tiresome as the pictures in the A B C, although once they had been endlessly new. Here Niels and the pastor's Frithjof had rolled a barrel-hoop. The hoop was a ship: if it fell over, that meant shipwreck; if you caught it first, the ship was dropping anchor. The gap between the outbuildings, so tight you could scarcely pass through, was Bab-el-Mandeb, the Portal of Death. Chalk letters named the stable door “England” and the barn door “France.” The garden gate became Rio Janeiro, while the smithy was Brazil. They also played Holger the Dane. You _could_ manage that among the tall burs behind the barn, but up in the miller's pasture were two sink-holes called the gorges. There the real Prince Burmand and his fierce Saracens lurked, wearing reddish-grey turbans and yellow helmet-plumes: the tallest burdocks and Aaron's rod. That alone was _real_ Mauretania. Those lush, fleshy stalks, that mass of vigorous, crowded life, roused a craving to destroy and made destruction a sensual delight. Their wooden swords flashed like steel. Green sap became red blood on the blades, and the severed stems crushed beneath their feet were Turkish bodies under horses' hoofs, making the sound of bones crunching inside flesh.

Sometimes the game moved down to the fjord. They floated mussel-shell ships; a vessel caught in seaweed or grounded on a sandbar became Columbus in the Sargasso Sea, or the discovery of America. They constructed harbours and huge embankments and carved the Nile through the firm sand of the shore. Once they built Gurre Castle from pebbles. A tiny dead fish laid in an oyster-shell was Tove's body, and they were King Valdemar, sitting beside her in grief.
All that belonged to the past now.

Niels was a proper lad, twelve and approaching thirteen. He no longer had to slash thistles and burdocks to sustain his dreams of knighthood, or float an explorer's hopes in a mussel-shell. A book and a sofa corner now sufficed. If the book would not carry him to the shore he longed for, he sought out Frithjof and told him the story it had failed to provide. Arm in arm they strolled along the road, one speaking and both listening. For complete abandon, when they wanted their imaginations to run utterly free, they hid in the hayloft's fragrant half-light. In time these stories, always stopping just as you had truly entered them, joined into one long, endless tale, living and dying through successive generations. When a hero aged, or you carelessly allowed him to die, he could always leave a son. The son inherited everything his father had, and could be given whatever further virtues you happened to prize most at that particular moment.

Everything that impressed itself on Niels entered the story: what he saw, what he understood or misunderstood, what he admired, and what he knew he was supposed to admire. Flowing water takes colour from each passing image. Sometimes it reflects it perfectly, sometimes twists it or returns it in wavering outlines, and sometimes swallows it entirely in the movement and colour of its own ripples. So, as best it could, the boy's tale reflected thoughts and feelings, his own and other people's; it mirrored people and events, books and life. An imagined life ran alongside the real one. Here was a safe, warm refuge for surrendering to the wildest adventures; a fairy garden that opened at the smallest nod and welcomed you into its splendour, leaving everyone else outside. Palms whispered together overhead. At your feet, vines of coral spread leaves like stars and flowers of sunlight, and a thousand paths led among them to every climate and age. One path took you here, another there: to Aladdin and Robinson Crusoe, Vaulunder and Henrik Magnard, Niels Klim and Mungo Park, Peter Simple and Odysseus. Whenever you wished, you could be home again in an instant.
Roughly a month after Niels turned twelve, two unfamiliar faces arrived at Lönborggaard.
One belonged to a new tutor. The other belonged to Edele Lyhne.

The tutor, Mr. Bigum, was a candidate for orders, nearly forty. Short, but solidly strong as a work-horse, he had a broad chest, high shoulders, and a slight stoop. His steps were slow, heavy, and deliberate. His arms moved vaguely, without expression, seeming to need a surprising amount of space. His forehead was high and wide, flat as a wall, with two vertical creases between the brows. He had a short, blunt nose and a large mouth with thick, fresh lips. His finest feature was his eyes: pale, gentle, and clear. The way they moved betrayed a slight deafness. Still, he loved music and played the violin with passionate dedication. Notes, he maintained, were heard not just through the ears but through the whole body—eyes, fingers, feet. When hearing failed, the hand could locate the right note unaided, guided by a strange intuitive genius of its own. Besides, audible notes were false in any case. Anyone endowed with the divine gift of music possessed an invisible instrument within, beside which even the finest Cremona resembled a savage's stringed calabash. On that inner instrument the soul performed. Its strings sounded ideal notes; on it the great poets of music had composed their immortal works.

Outward music, carried through real air and received by real ears, was only a pitiful imitation, a stammering effort to express the inexpressible. It resembled the soul's music only as a statue fashioned by hands, cut with a chisel and checked with a measure, resembled the sculptor's marvellous dream in marble—a dream no eyes had ever seen and no lips had praised.

Music was far from Mr. Bigum's principal concern, however. Above all he was a philosopher, though not one of those productive philosophers who discover laws and construct systems. Their systems made him laugh: snail-shells in which they hauled themselves over thought's boundless fields, imagining all the while that the fields were inside their shells! And their laws—laws of nature, laws of thought! Discovering a law meant only defining your own limits: this far I can see, no farther. As though beyond the first horizon there were not a second, and then another, and another still, horizon after horizon and law after law stretching endlessly away! That was not his kind of philosophy. He did not consider himself vain or inclined to exaggerate his worth, but the greater reach of his intelligence, compared with other mortals', was a fact he could not deny. Reading the great thinkers, he seemed to stride through a country inhabited by sleeping giants of thought. Bathed in his spirit's light, they awoke to an awareness of their own power. It always happened so. Any other person's thought, feeling, or mood privileged to awaken in him rose bearing his mark on its forehead: nobler, purer, stronger-winged, granted a force and majesty its own creator had never imagined.

How often he had contemplated his soul's marvellous riches and his spirit's divine certainty in almost humble wonder! On different days he might view the world and all it contained from utterly opposing positions, through assumptions as far apart as morning and night. Yet the positions and assumptions he adopted never took possession of him, even for a second. A god may clothe himself in the shape of a bull or swan, but he does not thereby become a bull or swan and stop being divine. So it was with him.

Nobody guessed what he carried within; they all walked past without seeing. Their blindness pleased him, feeding his contempt for humanity. One day the light would leave his eyes, and the magnificent architecture of his mind would collapse to its foundations, as though it had never existed. Yet no work of his, not a single line, would survive to reveal what had perished with him. His genius would wear neither the thorn-crown of the world's misunderstanding nor the stained purple robe of its applause. He exulted in imagining generations born and buried, and the greatest men of every age wasting years in pursuit of what he could have handed them simply by opening his palm.

His humble way of living gave him a peculiar pleasure. To spend a mind like his on teaching children was such magnificent waste; to exchange his time for daily bread was so wildly disproportionate. More absurd still, he earned that bread on recommendations from commonplace mortals, who had assured others that he knew enough to undertake a tutor's wretched duties. And in the examination for his degree they had awarded him _non_!

Oh, what delight in contemplating the brutal stupidity of a life that discarded him as worthless chaff and treasured empty husks as golden grain, while he knew his slightest thought outweighed a whole world!
At other moments, though, the loneliness of being so great pressed heavily on him and darkened his spirits.

Ah, so often after hours of holy, silent communion with himself, he returned to awareness of the audible, visible world and felt foreign to its smallness and decay. He was like the monk who heard a single phrase of the bird of paradise singing in the monastery woods, then came back to find a hundred years had passed. But if that monk felt lonely among a generation living in his familiar groves, how much lonelier must be the man whose own contemporaries had yet to be born.

In these desolate moods a cowardly wish sometimes overtook him: to descend to the common crowd's level, share its low-born happiness, become a native of its great earth and a citizen of its little heaven. Before long, however, he recovered himself.

The second arrival, Edele Lyhne, was Lyhne's twenty-six-year-old sister. For years she had lived in Copenhagen, initially with her mother, who moved there on becoming a widow. After her mother's death she joined the household of a rich uncle, Councillor of State Neergaard. The Neergaards entertained lavishly and went out constantly, carrying Edele through a whirl of festivities and balls.

Everywhere she went she attracted admiration, accompanied by its faithful shadow, envy. Without doing anything scandalous, she was discussed as much as anyone could be. Whenever men debated the town's three reigning beauties, many argued for removing one name and putting Edele Lyhne in its place. But they never agreed which of two women should make way for her. The third was beyond question.

Very young men, however, did not admire her. In her presence they lost confidence and felt twice as foolish as usual. She listened with mild tolerance, a tolerance so maliciously apparent that it crushed them with the knowledge that she had heard every word before and knew it by heart. Trying to shine both for her and for themselves, they adopted _blasés_ airs, invented extravagant paradoxes, or, at the height of desperation, made daring declarations. These efforts crowded and jostled each other in youth's sudden shifts of manner. She met them all with the faintest suggestion of a smile, lethally bored, which sent the victim blushing into the conviction that he was the hundred-and-eleventh fly in that same pitiless spider's web.
Besides, her beauty possessed neither the softness nor the fire that captures young hearts. For older hearts and cooler minds, it held a distinctive fascination.

She was tall. Her abundant, heavy blonde hair carried the faint red lustre of ripening wheat, turning lighter and curly where it grew in two points low at the back of her neck. Beneath a high, clearly shaped forehead, her eyebrows were faint and indistinct. Her large light-grey eyes were clear, neither emphasized by those brows nor given shifting shadows by their thin, delicate lids. Something in their expression could neither be determined nor defined. They always looked directly and openly at you, without darting flashes or the changeful play of sideways glances. Almost unnaturally alert, they were unconquerable and unreadable. All the animation belonged to the lower face: nostrils, mouth, and chin. The eyes simply watched. Her mouth was especially expressive, the lips meeting in a beautiful bow of deep, graceful curves and supple lines. A certain hardness in the lower lip slightly spoiled that beauty. Sometimes it dissolved into a smile; at other times it stiffened into something almost brutal.

The daring curve of her back and the sumptuous fullness of her breast contrasted with the classical restraint of shoulders and arms. Together they lent her a boldness, an exotic allure, heightened by the shining whiteness of her skin and the unhealthy redness of her lips. She provoked and unsettled the beholder.

There was a subtle distinction in her tall, slender body. She knew how to emphasize it with deliberate, confident artistry, especially in her ball dresses. Indeed, that artistic feeling for her own appearance sometimes proclaimed itself so loudly in her clothes that even their most exquisite taste came close to suggesting bad taste. For many people this merely increased her charm.

Her conduct could not have been more scrupulously proper. In her own words and in what she allowed others to say, she observed prudery's strictest limits. Her way of flirting was never to flirt: to remain hopelessly unaware of her power, and to favour none of her admirers in the slightest. That was precisely why all of them dreamed intoxicatingly about the face concealed beneath the mask. They imagined fire under snow, detected corruption within innocence. Learning that she kept a secret lover would have surprised none of them, but none would have dared suggest who he might be.
That was the Edele Lyhne people believed they saw.

She had come from the city to Lönborggaard because the endless pleasures, the thousand and one nights of dancing and masquerades, had damaged her health. Late in the winter the doctor found her lungs affected and ordered fresh air, quiet, and milk. Her new home supplied all three in abundance. It also supplied relentless boredom, and within a week she was longing for Copenhagen. Letter after letter pleaded for permission to end her exile; she suggested that homesickness injured her more than the fresh air helped. But the doctor had frightened her aunt and uncle so thoroughly that they believed duty required them to ignore her appeals, however moving.

What she missed was not chiefly the social entertainment. She craved the feeling of her life merging with the city's air, crowded with sounds. In the country everything was still—thoughts, words, eyes—and she seemed to hear herself continuously, with a clarity she could not escape, as one hears a clock tick throughout a sleepless night. Worse was knowing that over there life went on exactly as before. It was as though she lay dead in the night's silence, listening to music from a ballroom drifting across her grave.

She had nobody to talk to. Not one person caught the precise shade of meaning that gave her words their point. Naturally they understood her in a sense, since she spoke Danish, but vaguely and broadly, as they might understand a foreign language heard only occasionally. A certain inflection never told them who or what she meant. They failed to recognize a phrase as a quotation, or another, delivered in that particular way, as a fresh variation on a current joke. Their own speech had a respectable thinness through which you could practically feel its grammatical ribs. They used words so literally that the words might have just stepped out of a dictionary column. Even their pronunciation of Copenhagen! Sometimes it bore a mysterious weight, as though people ate little children there. Sometimes they looked far away, as if naming a city in central Africa, or adopted a ceremonial tone trembling with history, as for Nineveh or Carthage. The pastor invariably called it Axelstead, with the tender rapture of remembering a former sweetheart. None could say Copenhagen and mean the city running from Vesterport to the Custom House, on either side of Östergade and Kongens Nytorv. The same fault ran through everything they did and said.

Nothing at Lönborggaard pleased her: all those meals timed by the sun, lavender smells from chests and cupboards, Spartan chairs, all that provincial furniture cowering along the walls as though frightened of people! Even the air offended her. A walk always sent her home steeped in a hearty scent of meadow hay and wildflowers, as if she had been shut inside a haymarket.
And then there was being called aunt—Aunt Edele. How harshly it sounded in her ears! She grew accustomed to it eventually, but at first it put a chill between her and Niels.
Niels was not bothered.

One Sunday early in August, Lyhne and his wife drove out in their carriage to visit someone, leaving Niels and Miss Edele at home. That morning she had asked him to gather corn-flowers for her, and he had forgotten. In the afternoon, walking with Frithjof, he suddenly remembered, picked a bouquet, and ran back to the house.

The house was so quiet that he thought his aunt must be sleeping, and he tiptoed through it. At the sitting-room entrance he paused, holding his breath before approaching Edele's door. Sunshine filled the room; a flowering oleander saturated the air with sweetness. The only sound was a soft splash from the flower-stand whenever the goldfish shifted in their glass bowl.

With arms extended for balance and tongue caught between his teeth, Niels crossed the room. He carefully took the doorknob, hot enough in the sunshine to burn his hand, and turned it slowly, frowning and half shutting his eyes. Drawing the door towards him, he leaned through the narrow gap and placed the bouquet on a chair just inside. The room was dark, as though its blinds had been lowered, and the air seemed damp with perfume—attar of roses. Bent over, he could see only pale straw matting, the panelling beneath the window, and the lacquered base of a Gueridon. When he straightened to back out, however, he saw his aunt.

She lay at full length on a sea-green satin couch, wearing a fanciful gypsy costume. Her back rested flat, her chin lifted, her throat stretched, and her forehead low. Loosened hair streamed over the couch's end and across the rug. An artificial pomegranate flower seemed to have washed ashore on an island formed by a small bronze-coloured shoe amid that muted golden current.

The mingled colours of her clothes were rich and soft. Muted blue, pale pink, grey, and orange ran together in the pattern of a small, low-cut bodice made of thick, matt fabric. Beneath it was a white silk chemise whose loose sleeves reached her elbows. Its white carried a faint pink cast, threaded with reddish gold. A borderless skirt of pansy-coloured velvet lay loosely gathered around her, slipping in diagonal folds over the couch's edge. Her legs and feet were uncovered; around her crossed ankles she had looped a necklace of pale coral. An unfolded fan lay on the floor, displaying playing-cards arranged like a wheel. Farther away lay a pair of leaf-brown silk stockings, one partly rolled, the other stretched out to reveal its red clock embroidery.

She noticed Niels at the very instant he noticed her. Almost involuntarily she stirred as if to get up, then stopped and remained lying where she was. Only her head turned slightly, and she looked at him with an inquiring smile.
“I've brought these for you,” he said, carrying the flowers across to her.
She reached out, looked from the bouquet to her clothes as though matching the colours, then let it fall with a tired murmur: “Impossible!”
Niels started to retrieve the flowers, but a movement of her hand stopped him.
“Pass me that!” she said, indicating a red flask on a crumpled handkerchief beside her feet.

He went to fetch it. Bending over the gently rounded, milk-white legs and the long, narrow feet, whose fine, flexible lines seemed almost as expressive as a hand, he turned crimson. Dizziness overcame him. When one foot suddenly moved, turning and bending downwards, he nearly lost his balance.
Edele asked, “Where did you find those flowers?”
Niels collected himself and turned her way. “In the pastor's rye-field,” he answered, hearing a voice he scarcely recognized as his own. He gave her the flask, keeping his eyes lowered.

His agitation puzzled Edele, and she stared at him. Then she suddenly blushed, lifted herself on one arm, and tucked her feet beneath her petticoat. “Go, go, go, go!” she said, partly cross and partly embarrassed, spraying him with attar of roses at each word.
Niels left. Once he was gone, she slowly lowered her feet from the couch and studied them with curiosity.

He ran unsteadily through the house to his room. He felt dazed, strangely weak at the knees, with a tightness in his throat. Flinging himself onto the couch, he shut his eyes, but that did no good. An unfamiliar restlessness took hold; he breathed heavily as if frightened, and the light hurt him even through his closed lids.

Gradually he began to feel different. Something like a hot, heavy breath passed over him, leaving him helplessly weak. He was like a dreamer who hears a summons and tries to respond but cannot move a foot. His helplessness torments him; longing to escape makes him sick; the voice, unaware that he is bound, calls him towards madness. Niels sighed impatiently like someone ill, looking around without knowing where to turn. Never before had he felt so wretched, so alone, so abandoned and lost.
He sat where sunlight poured through the window and began to cry.

After that day, being near Edele brought Niels a shy happiness. She was no longer an ordinary person but something exalted, made divine by her mysterious, extraordinary beauty. Merely looking at her filled him with rapture. Inwardly he knelt before her, crawled to her feet, erased himself in devotion. Yet sometimes this worship needed outward gestures of submission. Then he watched for an opportunity to slip into her room and perform an established ritual: a seemingly endless, fixed number of kisses bestowed on the little rug beside her bed, a shoe, or whatever else offered itself as an object of his idolatry.

It seemed extraordinarily fortunate that just then his Sunday jacket was relegated to everyday wear. The remaining perfume of attar of roses acted as a powerful talisman, summoning in a magic mirror the image of Edele on the green couch in her masquerade dress. That image now haunted the story he shared with Frithjof. From this point on, poor Frithjof was never secure against barefoot princesses. Struggling through dense, ancient forest, he heard them call from hammocks woven of vines. Taking refuge from a storm in a mountain cave, he saw them rise from beds of velvety moss to greet him. Even when he burst into a pirate's cabin, bloodied and black with smoke, smashing the door with a mighty sabre-stroke, they awaited him on the captain's green sofa. He found them dreadfully boring and could not understand why their favourite heroes suddenly had to encounter them everywhere.

However high a person builds his throne, however firmly he settles on his brow the tiara of exceptional gifts—of genius—he can never be entirely certain he is safe from suddenly wanting, like Nebuchadnezzar, to drop to all fours, eat grass, and mingle with the ordinary beasts of the field.

That was Mr. Bigum's fate when he quite simply fell in love with Miss Edele. Twisting history to justify his attachment did not help. He might call her Beatrice, Laura, or Vittoria Colonna, but every artificial halo he lit around his love went out at once before the stubborn truth: he loved Edele's beauty. Nor had the qualities of her mind or heart enchanted him. He loved her elegance, her fashionable manner, her effortless assurance, even the grace of her insolence. Such a love might well leave him ashamed and astonished at the fickleness of human creatures.

And what difference did any of it make! His eternal truths and improvised lies, linked ring by ring into the heavy armour he called principles—what were they beside love? If they truly were life's strength, marrow, and core, let them demonstrate their power. If weaker, let them shatter; if stronger—But they had shattered already, pulled apart like the rotten web of threads they were. What did eternal truth mean to her? What use were his mighty visions? Could thoughts that sounded the unfathomable win her over? Everything he owned was worthless. His soul might shine with a hundred suns, but what good was that if its light remained concealed beneath the ugly fustian of Diogenes' cloak? Oh, to be beautiful! Take my soul and pay me my thirty pieces of silver—Alcibiades' body, Don Juan's cloak, the rank of a court chamberlain!

Unfortunately, he possessed none of those attractions, and Edele felt no pull towards his ponderous philosophical nature. His habit of reducing life to crudely bare abstractions made him loudly dogmatic, unpleasantly certain. He jarred on her like a drum intruding into a concert of quiet music. His mind was always straining, flexing its muscles and striking a pose over the smallest question, like a strongman preparing to juggle iron balls; she found it ridiculous. His censorious morality annoyed her too. It pounced on each lightly suggested feeling as it drifted through conversation, stripped away its disguise, and rudely announced its name just as it was about to pass him by.

Bigum knew perfectly well how unfavourably he appeared and how hopeless his love must be. But he knew it as we know something we hope, with every force of the soul, will prove untrue. There is still the possibility of a miracle. Miracles do not happen, yet they might. Who can say? Intelligence, instinct, and senses may mislead us, for all their daylight clarity. Perhaps all that is needed is irrational courage, following hope's will-o'-the-wisp as it flickers above boiling passions heavy with desire! Only when destiny's door slams shut do we feel certainty's icy talons entering our breast, closing slowly, slowly round the heart. They seize the delicate thread of hope from which our whole happy world is suspended. The thread snaps; everything it held falls and breaks; a cry of despair rings through the emptiness.
While doubt remains, despair cannot be complete.

One sunny September afternoon, Edele sat on the landing above the half-dozen broad, old-fashioned steps from the summer parlour to the garden. Behind her, the French windows stood wide open against a covering of bright red and green climbing leaves. Resting her head against a chair stacked with large black portfolios, she held an etching up in both hands. Coloured prints of Byzantine mosaics, blue and gold, lay scattered over the landing's pale-green rush matting, across the threshold, and onto the parlour's oak-brown parquet. A white shade hat lay at the bottom of the steps. Her hair was bare except for a flower of gold filigree matching the design of the bracelet worn high on her arm. Her white dress, made from a partly transparent fabric with narrow silky stripes, was edged in twisted orange-and-black chenille and small rosettes of those colours. Thin silk mitts stretched from her hands to her elbows, pearl-grey like her shoes.

Yellow sunshine filtered through the hanging branches of an old ash tree. Shafts of light pierced the cool shade, sprinkling gold dust through the air and dappling steps, wall, and doors: patch upon patch of sun, as through a pierced screen. Through the pattern of shadow, every colour lifted towards the light. White rose from Edele's dress, blood-red from her crimson lips, amber from her yellow-blonde hair. Around her answered a hundred other shades: blue and gold, oak-brown, gleaming glass, red and green.

Edele let the etching drop and looked up unhappily. Her eyes voiced a silent complaint she was too tired even to sigh. Then she sank back again, as though withdrawing into herself and shutting the surrounding world away.
At that moment Mr. Bigum came into view.
She watched him with sleepy, blinking eyes, like a child too drowsy and comfortable to move, but too curious to close its eyes altogether.

Mr. Bigum had put on his new beaver hat. Lost in thought, he waved his tombac watch so vigorously that its slender silver chain seemed about to break. Then, with a sudden, almost savage gesture, he pushed the watch far into his pocket, flung back his head impatiently, and seized his coat lapel in an irritated grip. He was about to hurry on with a furious jerk of his whole body. His face darkened with that hopeless rage which seethes in someone fleeing his own tormenting thoughts and knowing flight is useless.

Edele's hat halted his escape. It shone white at the steps' foot against the path's black earth. Picking it up in both hands, he saw Edele, then stood holding it instead of returning it, struggling for something to say. His mind produced no idea; his tongue could bring forth no word. He stared ahead with the foolish look of profundity brought to a sudden stop.
To end the awkward silence, Edele remarked casually, “It's a hat, Mr. Bigum.”
“Yes,” the tutor replied eagerly, pleased that she had confirmed a resemblance he too had noticed. An instant later the clumsiness of his reply made him blush.

“It was here,” he rushed on, “on the ground here, like this—exactly here.” Bending down, he showed its former position with a pointless precision born of embarrassment. The relief of having shown some sign of life, however useless, made him almost happy. Still he stood there holding the hat.
Edele asked, “Are you planning to keep it?”
To this Bigum could find no reply.
“I mean, would you hand it to me?” she clarified.

Bigum stepped closer and offered the hat. “Miss Lyhne,” he began, “you think—you mustn't think—I beg you to hear me; that is, I haven't said anything, but please be patient! I love you, Miss Lyhne, beyond utterance, beyond utterance, beyond anything words can express. Oh, if there were a word that held a slave's abject admiration, a martyr's ecstatic smile, and an exile's consuming homesickness, that word would tell you how I love. Oh, hear me out; don't send me away yet! Don't suppose some mad hope has made me insult you! I know how little I am in your eyes, how awkward and repellent—yes, repellent. I haven't forgotten my poverty. You must know how poor I am: my mother has to live in a charitable institution, and I can do nothing, nothing, to change it. I am miserably poor. Yes, Miss Lyhne, here I am only a humble servant in your brother's house. Yet in another world I reign, powerful, proud, wealthy, crowned with victory, ennobled by the same passion that sent Prometheus to steal fire from the gods' heaven. There I am brother to all the great spirits the earth has produced, the spirits who themselves sustain the earth. I understand them as equals alone understand each other. Their highest flight never rises beyond what my wings can reach. Do you understand? Do you believe me? Oh, don't believe a word! None of it is true. I am only the Kobold figure standing here before you. All that is over. This dreadful madness of love has crippled my wings, blinded my spirit's eyes, dried my heart, and drained my soul into bloodless cowardice. Oh, Miss Lyhne, save me from myself; don't turn from me in contempt! Weep for me, weep—Rome is burning!”

He had dropped to his knees on the steps and was twisting his hands together. His face was white and contorted, his teeth clenched with pain, his eyes swimming in tears. His whole body trembled with stifled sobs, audible only in his gasps for air.

“Compose yourself, Mr. Bigum,” she said with a touch too much pity. “Compose yourself; don't collapse like this—be a man! Please stand up, walk in the garden for a little while, and try to recover yourself.”

Barely audibly, Mr. Bigum groaned, “And you can't love me even a little? Oh, how dreadful! There is nothing in my soul I wouldn't kill or degrade to win you. No, no, if someone offered me madness, with the chance of possessing you in my hallucinations—_possessing_ you—I would say: Take my brain. Smash its marvellous architecture with rough hands. Snap every delicate thread binding my spirit to human thought's radiant triumphal chariot. Let me sink into the body's mire beneath its wheels, while others follow those shining roads towards the light! Do you understand? Can you imagine it? Even if your love came stripped of glory, degraded, filthy, a grotesque imitation, a sick mind's phantom, I would fall on my knees and receive it like the Sacred Host. But the best of me is useless, and so is the worst. I appeal to the sun and get no light; to the statue and get no answer—answer!... What answer is there, beyond my suffering? No, this agony that tears me to my deepest roots, these unspeakable torments throughout my being, are merely an impertinence to you. All you feel is a little chilly offence. Secretly you laugh at the poor tutor and his absurd passion.”

Edele stood, and Mr. Bigum got up too. “You are unfair to me,” she said. “I'm not laughing. You ask whether there is any hope, and I tell you there is none. Surely that's no cause for laughter. But I have something to tell you. From the moment you first began thinking about me, you must have known my answer. You did know, didn't you? You knew throughout, yet you drove every desire and thought towards a goal you knew was impossible. Your love doesn't offend me, Mr. Bigum, but I condemn it. You have done what so many do: shut your eyes to reality and refuse to listen when life says ‘No’ to what you want. People try to forget the gulf fate has put between themselves and the thing they desperately desire. They demand the fulfilment of their dreams. But life pays no attention to dreams. Not one obstacle can be dreamed away. In the end we are left weeping at the edge of that gulf, still unchanged and exactly where it was. We, though, have changed. We've allowed our dreams to drive our thoughts and spur our desires to the highest possible pitch. The gulf hasn't narrowed, and everything within us clamours to cross it. But the answer is no, always no, never anything different. If only we had watched ourselves while there was time! Now it's too late, and we are unhappy.”
She stopped, almost as if coming out of a trance. Her voice had been quiet and searching, as though she were talking to herself. Now it grew hard, cold, and distant.

“I can't help you, Mr. Bigum. You are none of the things you wish to be to me. If that makes you miserable, then you must be miserable; if you suffer, then you must suffer. Somebody always has to suffer. Make a person your God and master of your destiny, and you must submit to that deity's will. But inventing gods for yourself is never wise, nor is surrendering your soul to someone else. Some gods refuse to descend from their pedestals. Be reasonable, Mr. Bigum! Your god is so small, so unworthy of devotion. Turn away and find happiness with one of the daughters of the land.”

With a slight smile, she went inside through the summer parlour. Mr. Bigum watched her go, crushed. For another quarter of an hour he paced before the steps. The words they had spoken seemed still to tremble in the air. She had left so recently that surely her shadow must remain, surely his pleas could still reach her, surely the end could not yet be irrevocable. At last, however, the chambermaid came out. She gathered the prints and carried away the chair, portfolios, rush matting—everything.
After that, he too could leave.

Above, at the open gable window, Niels sat watching him. He had overheard the conversation from its first word to its last. Fear showed in his face; a nervous shudder ran through his body. For the first time, life frightened him. For the first time he understood that when life condemns you to pain, it is neither an invention nor an empty threat. You _are_ hauled to the rack; you _are_ tortured. No miraculous rescue arrives in the final instant, and you do not wake as from a nightmare.
The realization came as a warning that filled him with terror.

Edele's autumn was a bad one, and winter exhausted what remained of her strength. When spring arrived, it found not one small seed of life to warm and encourage into growth. There was only a withering that neither gentleness nor warmth could stop, or even slow. Spring could still flood that fading life with light and soothe its ebbing strength with sweet, mild air, as evening's crimson slowly follows the dying day.

The end arrived in May, on a day full of sunshine, when the lark never stopped singing and the rye seemed almost visibly to grow. Beyond her window the great cherry-trees stood white with blossom: snowy bouquets, snowy wreaths, domes and arches and garlands, an architecture of enchantment against the deepest blue sky.
She was extremely weak that day, yet felt strangely light. She knew the end was near: that morning she had called for Bigum to say farewell.

Her uncle had travelled from Copenhagen. Throughout the afternoon the handsome white-haired man sat beside her bed, his hand enclosed in both of hers. He said nothing. Occasionally he moved his hand and she squeezed it; she raised her eyes and he smiled. Her brother was there as well, administering medicine and attending to her other needs.

Motionless, eyes closed, she let familiar scenes from her life over there pass before her. Sorgenfri and its trailing birches; Lyngby's red church rising on a foundation of graves; the white country house with the small sunken lane down to the sea, where the fence stayed green as if the water had painted it. The pictures formed, sharpened, dissolved, and disappeared. Others followed. Bredgade at sunset, darkness gathering about the houses. That strange Copenhagen encountered on returning from the country before noon, oddly busy and hurried in the sunshine, its windowpanes whitened, its streets smelling of fruit. In the strong light the houses seemed unreal; even the clatter of wheels could not dispel the silence wrapped around them.... Then the quiet, dim drawing room on autumn evenings, when she was dressed for the theatre but the others had not come downstairs—the scent of incense, the stove's wood fire casting light on the carpet, rain lashing the windows, horses stamping outside, the sad calls of mussel-venders ... and behind it all the waiting theatre, full of brightness, music, and festive warmth.
The afternoon slipped by amid these remembered pictures.

Niels and his mother waited in the parlour. Kneeling beside the sofa, his face buried in its brown velvet, he clasped his hands above his head. He cried and wailed openly, yielding to grief without any effort to restrain it. Mrs. Lyhne sat next to him. On the table before her lay an open hymn-book, turned to the hymns usually sung at funerals. From time to time she read a few verses. Sometimes she leaned towards her son with a soothing word or a rebuke. But comfort could not reach him, and she could stop neither his tears nor the desperate, wild prayers he uttered.

After a while Lyhne appeared at the sickroom door. He made no gesture, but the gravity of his look brought them both to their feet. They followed him to his sister. Taking their hands, he led them to the bed. Edele looked up, gazing at each in turn, her lips trying to form words. Lyhne then brought his wife to a seat by the window. Niels fell to his knees at the bed's foot.

He cried quietly, hands clasped, pouring out prayer after prayer in an urgent, passionate whisper. He told God he refused to surrender hope. “I won't let You go, Lord. Not until You've answered ‘Yes’! You mustn't take her from us. You know how much we love her—You mustn't, You mustn't! Oh, I can't say ‘Thy will be done,’ because You want to let her die—but let her live! I'll obey You and thank You. Whatever I know You want, I'll do. I'll be good, I'll never offend You, only let her stay alive! Can You hear, God? Oh, stop, stop—make her well before there isn't time! I will, I will—oh, what is there I can promise? Oh, I'll thank You, I'll never, never forget You, but please hear me! Can't You see she's dying? She's dying—can't You see? Do You hear? Take Your hand off her! God, I can't lose her, I can't! Please let her live, please, please? Oh, You're being wicked—”

Outside the window, sunset turned the white blossoms pink. Arch after arch, the flowering branches made a castle of roses from their delicate bloom, a vaulted choir of roses. Through that airy dome the sky's azure softened into evening blue. Golden lights, and lights of gold blazing into crimson, sprang like a halo's rays from every garlanded outline of the weightless temple.
Edele lay white and quiet, both hands still holding the old man's. Slowly, breath by breath, life left her. Her breast rose ever more faintly; her eyelids sank ever more heavily.
Her last faint whisper was, “My love to Copenhagen!”

Yet her final message reached nobody. Not even a breath carried it past her lips. It was meant for him, the great artist she had loved in secret with all her soul. To him she had meant nothing: only a familiar-sounding name, an unrecognized figure among the great crowd of his admirers.
Light dwindled into blue twilight, and her hands slackened and parted. The shadows deepened, shadows of night and death.
The old man leaned over the bed and set his hands against her pulse, waiting in silence. When the last stirring of life had ebbed and the final weak beat stopped, he raised the pale hand to his lips.
“Little Edele!”
